opus-5.5.text:
I think the key is actually somewhat counterintuitive: to use simulation effectively, you first need to be really good at learning from real-world data. People often think of simulation as a substitute for real experience, a way to avoid the cost of collecting data on physical robots. But in my experience it works best as an amplifier for a system that already has a strong foundation grounded in reality.

Here's why. If your model doesn't understand how the real world works, it has no way of knowing which parts of the simulation matter and which are artifacts. Every simulator is wrong in some ways. The friction isn't quite right, the contact dynamics are off, the visuals look different. A model trained mostly in simulation will happily exploit those quirks. But a model with a rich, real-world-grounded representation can treat the simulator more like a person treats imagination or a video game. You know it's not real, but you can still extract useful lessons because you have a frame of reference to interpret them.

It's a bit like how people learn. Someone who's never driven a car doesn't get much out of a driving simulator, but an experienced driver can practice emergency maneuvers in one and transfer that skill, because they already know what driving feels like and can mentally fill in the gaps.

So I think the path forward is to build models that learn from large amounts of diverse real-world experience, robot data, but also video, human demonstrations, and all sorts of other sources, so they develop general representations of physical interaction. Once you have that, simulation, synthetic data, and other auxiliary sources become much more valuable, because the model can use them to fill in specific gaps: rare failure cases, dangerous situations, or reasoning about counterfactuals. The real-world foundation tells the model how to read the auxiliary data, rather than the auxiliary data having to stand on its own.

The other piece is that the learning algorithms need to handle data of varying quality and relevance. The same machinery that lets a model learn from suboptimal real-world data, figuring out what to keep and what to discount, is what lets it absorb simulated or off-domain data without being misled by it. That's partly why I think reinforcement learning and related methods that reason about outcomes, rather than just imitating, will be important here.

r001.rationale: It says effective use of simulation and auxiliary data depends on first building a strong foundation from real-world data.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss meta-learning or suggest that such an ability may emerge without an explicit meta-learning procedure.

r003.rationale: It links a real-world foundation to using synthetic data, but does not identify LLMs or explain their use of synthetic data.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the key is that the model has to be able to decide for itself how much to trust each source of data, and it has to be able to make that decision based on what it actually experiences in the real world. The reason simulation and other auxiliary data have been hard to use isn't that they're useless. It's that they're useful in ways that are hard to predict in advance. A simulator might be very accurate about the geometry of a scene and completely wrong about contact dynamics or the way a cloth deforms. If you hand-design the split, if you say "trust the simulation for this and the real data for that," you'll get it wrong, and you'll get it wrong in different ways for every task.

So what I think we want is something closer to how a person uses a flight simulator or a textbook. You don't memorize the textbook and then act as if the world is the textbook. You extract the parts that transfer and then you calibrate against reality. For a learning system, that means the real-world data has to be the ground truth that everything else is grounded in, and the auxiliary data acts more like a prior. It tells you what's plausible, it narrows down the space of behaviors, and then a relatively small amount of real experience tells you which of those plausible behaviors actually works.

The second ingredient, and I think this is underrated, is that the model has to be able to improve from its own experience, not just from a fixed dataset. Because the mismatch between simulation and the world isn't something you fix once. The robot goes out, it does things, some of them fail, and that failure is exactly the signal that tells you where the simulation was lying to you. If the model can close that loop, if it can go from "this is what I expected, this is what happened" to an updated understanding, then the auxiliary data becomes a starting point rather than a ceiling. If it can't close that loop, then you're perpetually stuck patching the simulator by hand, and that's a losing game.

So, in short: treat simulation and internet data and human video as a prior, treat real interaction as the thing that corrects the prior, and build the system so that the correction happens continually and automatically rather than through a human engineer deciding what to fix.

r001.rationale: The response makes real-world interaction the ground truth that calibrates auxiliary data and says the system should continually learn from its real-world experience to improve.

r002.rationale: It calls for the system to improve from experience but does not say that meta-learning may emerge without an explicit meta-learning procedure.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss LLMs or attribute their use of synthetic data to a foundation learned from real data.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that the model needs to be able to improve with experience. Simulation doesn’t have to reproduce the real world perfectly to be useful. It has to provide experience from which the model can learn something that carries over, and then the model needs to be able to use real-world experience to correct the things that don’t carry over.

If you train a policy entirely in simulation and then freeze it and deploy it, you’re asking a lot of the simulator. Every discrepancy becomes a potential failure. But if simulation gives you a starting point, and learning continues in the real world, then the question becomes: did the simulation make that subsequent learning faster?

I’d think about other auxiliary data in much the same way. Videos, demonstrations, simulated interactions—they provide different kinds of information. You don’t necessarily need each source to teach you the whole task. You need a learning process that can extract what’s useful from each and then refine it through interaction.

r001.rationale: The response says auxiliary data should help a model learn what carries over, then be refined through real-world experience, making subsequent real-world learning faster.

r002.rationale: It describes learning from varied sources but does not say the needed meta-learning ability may emerge without an explicit meta-learning procedure.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss LLMs or attribute effective use of synthetic data to a foundation learned from real data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that the model has to be able to improve from experience, rather than just imitate the data that you give it. Simulation is useful because you can try something, observe what happens, and use that outcome to change your behavior. But you need a learning process that can take advantage of that feedback.

For example, if you train a robot entirely in simulation and then put it in the real world, there will inevitably be things that the simulator gets wrong. One approach is to make the simulator more and more accurate. That helps, but I think the more general solution is to have a system that can use simulation to acquire a useful starting point, and then continue learning from real experience.

That also changes what you need from the auxiliary data. It doesn’t have to perfectly match the task or the environment. It has to teach you something useful that you can subsequently adapt. So I would put the emphasis on building that continuous learning loop, where simulated experience, prior data, and interaction with the real world can all contribute to improving the same model.

r001.rationale: The response says the key is a learning loop that uses simulation as a starting point and continues learning from real-world experience, connecting auxiliary data to better real-world performance.

r002.rationale: It does not say that meta-learning may emerge without an explicit meta-learning procedure.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss LLMs, synthetic data, or a foundation learned from real data.
